options.label: A
options.text: Right kidney, stomach, hepatic flexure of colon

options.label: B
options.text: Right kidney, stomach, splenic flexure of colon

options.label: C
options.text: Left kidney, stomach, splenic flexure of colon

options.label: D
options.text: Stomach, left kidney, splenic flexure of colon

questions.answerText: Stomach, left kidney, splenic flexure of colon
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Stomach, left kidney, splenic flexure of colon

 

The visceral surface of the spleen is anatomically related to several structures. These impressions help understand the organ's relationship with surrounding structures, crucial for both anatomy and surgery. The spleen's visceral surface is marked by:

 

A - Gastric impression: Related to the stomach, positioned anteromedially.

 

B - Renal impression: Related to the left kidney, positioned posteromedially.

 

C - Colic impression: Related to the splenic flexure of the colon, positioned inferiorly.

 

The mnemonic GCR (Girls Common Room) can help recall these impressions:

 

  • G: Gastric impression
  • C: Colic impression (splenic flexure of the colon)
  • R: Renal impression

 

Educational Objective:

 

The visceral surface of the spleen is related to three main structures: the stomach (gastric impression), left kidney (renal impression), and splenic flexure of the colon (colic impression). These relationships are critical during surgical approaches to the spleen.

questions.stem: During thoracotomy operation which structure is identified by beaded structure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Pecquet duct

 

The thoracic duct, also known as Pecquet duct, is a critical structure for lymphatic drainage and is identified during thoracotomy by its beaded appearance, which results from the presence of multiple valves along its length. These valves help regulate the flow of lymph and prevent backflow.

 

The thoracic duct collects lymph from most parts of the body, including the lower limbs, left upper limb, left side of the head and neck, and the left thorax, and drains into the left jugular-subclavian angle.

 

 

 

 

Key Features of the Thoracic Duct:

 

  • Length: Approximately 45 cm.
  • Course: Begins at the cisterna chyli (in the abdomen), ascends through the thoracic cavity, and terminates at the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins.
  • Changes direction at the T4-T5 junction
  • Function: Drains lymphatic fluid from the majority of the body except the right upper quadrant (drained by the right lymphatic duct).

 

The importance of the thoracic duct lies in its vital role in lymphatic circulation, and accidental damage during thoracic surgery can lead to severe complications, including chylothorax (accumulation of lymphatic fluid in the thoracic cavity).

 

Note:

 

Related mnemonics and structures:

 

  • Structures with 45 cm length:
    • Thoracic duct
    • Ductus deferens
    • Umbilical cord
    • Femur (longest bone in the thigh)
    • Sartorius muscle (longest muscle, "honeymoon muscle")
    • Spinal cord
    • Vertebral column (without intervertebral discs)
  • Structures with 25 cm length (mnemonic: DUDES):
    • Duodenum
    • Ureter
    • Esophagus
    • Stomach

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Esophagus: The esophagus is a muscular tube that connects the pharynx to the stomach. It does not have a beaded structure and lacks the multiple valves characteristic of the thoracic duct.

 

Option B. Ureter: The ureter is a tubular structure that transports urine from the kidney to the bladder. It is not visible in thoracotomy and does not exhibit a beaded structure.

 

Option D. Azygous vein: The azygous vein is a part of the venous system, running along the vertebral column. It appears as a smooth, tubular structure, not beaded.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The thoracic duct is identified during thoracotomy by its beaded appearance, caused by the presence of multiple valves, and drains lymph into the left jugular-subclavian angle.

questions.stem: During development of spiral valve in truncus arteriosus if abnormality occurs then it can result in Cyanotic heart diseases. Which of the following disease is related with this situation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) TOF

 

During heart development, the truncus arteriosus is divided into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk by the formation of a spiral septum. If the development of this spiral septum is abnormal or incomplete, it leads to cyanotic congenital heart diseases such as Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF).

 

 

TOF is characterized by four major defects ("tetra"):

 

  1. Pulmonary stenosis: Narrowing of the pulmonary valve or artery due to improper spiral septum formation.
  2. Overriding of the aorta: The aorta receives blood from both ventricles due to improper alignment.
  3. Ventricular septal defect (VSD): A hole in the septum between the right and left ventricles persists.
  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy: Due to increased pressure caused by pulmonary stenosis.

 

Development of Heart:

 

 

Mechanism:

 

  • Improper or unequal division of the truncus arteriosus by the spiral septum leads to a smaller pulmonary artery and a larger aorta, resulting in pulmonary stenosis and overriding of the aorta. These defects cause right-to-left shunting, leading to cyanosis.

 

 

 Variants:

 

  • Pentalogy of Fallot: Includes atrial septal defect (ASD).
  • Trilogy of Fallot: Absence of VSD.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. ASD (Atrial Septal Defect): ASD results from a defect in the atrial septum and is not directly linked to spiral septum abnormalities.

 

Option B. VSD (Ventricular Septal Defect): While a component of TOF, VSD alone is not the primary defect caused by abnormal truncus arteriosus development.

 

Option C. PDA (Patent Ductus Arteriosus): PDA occurs due to failure of the ductus arteriosus to close after birth and is unrelated to the spiral septum or truncus arteriosus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Abnormal development of the spiral valve in truncus arteriosus leads to Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), characterized by pulmonary stenosis, overriding of the aorta, VSD, and right ventricular hypertrophy. A classic radiological sign of TOF is the boot-shaped heart.

Ans. B) Microtome

 

The instrument shown in the image is a microtome, which is widely used in histopathology for slicing extremely thin sections of biological specimens. These thin slices are essential for preparing histology slides, which are then stained and examined under a microscope to study the microstructure of tissues.

 

  • The microtome uses a sharp knife and a precise mechanical system to produce uniform sections of paraffin-embedded tissue or frozen sections.
  • It is essential for diagnostic purposes, especially in pathology, to identify structural and cellular abnormalities.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Macrotome: Incorrect. A macrotome is not a standard instrument in histology and does not refer to a tool for preparing thin tissue sections.

 

Option C. L Mould: Incorrect. L moulds are used in embedding tissue samples during paraffin block preparation, not for slicing thin sections.

 

Option D. None: Incorrect. The correct identification of this instrument is the microtome.

The microtome is a crucial tool in histopathology, used to prepare ultra-thin tissue sections for microscopic examination.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not the lateral branch of abdominal aorta?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Inferior mesenteric artery 

 

Inferior mesenteric artery is the anterior branch of abdominal aorta


The abdominal aorta has three categories of branches based on their orientation: ventral, lateral, and dorsal. The lateral branches supply paired structures, such as the adrenal glands, kidneys, and gonads. A mnemonic to remember the lateral branches is "IMRT":

 

  • I: Inferior phrenic artery
  • M: Middle suprarenal artery
  • R: Renal artery
  • T: Testicular/Ovarian artery (gonadal artery)

 

The inferior mesenteric artery is a ventral branch of the abdominal aorta, supplying unpaired midline structures, such as the distal transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum.

 

Educational Objective:


The inferior mesenteric artery is a ventral branch of the abdominal aorta, while the lateral branches include the inferior phrenic, middle suprarenal, renal, and gonadal arteries.

 

Ventral branches are as follows

  1. Celiac trunk
  2. Superior mesenteric artery
  3. Inferior mesenteric artery

questions.stem: Type I Collagen is present in all except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Cartilage

 

Type I collagen is the most abundant collagen type in the human body and is predominantly found in tissues requiring high tensile strength. Here’s a breakdown:

 

Where Type I Collagen is Found:

 

  • Bone: It is the major collagen type in bone, providing structural integrity.
  • Aponeurosis: Aponeurosis is a flat, broad tendon, which, like tendons, is rich in Type I collagen.
  • Ligament: Ligaments, which connect bones to other bones, also have a high concentration of Type I collagen.

 

Cartilage: Cartilage is primarily composed of Type II collagen, which provides the tensile strength and elasticity required for joint and structural support. Though fibrocartilage contains type 1 collagen but in general the cartilage is made up of type 2 collagen.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Type I collagen is found in bone, aponeurosis, and ligaments, but cartilage is an exception as it primarily contains Type II collagen.

 

Other types of collagen and locations

  • Collagen 3 - Spleen, liver, lung
  • Collagen 4 - Basal lamina, kidney, lens capsule
  • Collagen 5 - placenta
  • Collagen 7 - Anchoring fibers in basement membrane

questions.stem: A 75 year old male presented with history of frequency, hesitancy & urgency for urination. He was on medication of Tamsulosin & Finasteride combination. Now Trans Urethral Resection of Prostate (TURP) surgery was recommended by physician. Why TURP is preferred over suprapubic prostectomy?

options.label: A
options.text: Prostatic venous plexus is located in between the true & false capsule of prostate & presented clinical condition involves peripheral zone of prostate.

options.label: B
options.text: Prostatic venous plexus is located below the true capsule of prostate & presented clinical condition involves peripheral zone of prostate.

options.label: C
options.text: Prostatic venous plexus is located in between the true & false capsule of prostate & presented clinical condition involves periurethral zone of prostate.

options.label: D
options.text: Prostatic venous plexus is located outside the false capsule of prostate & presented clinical condition involves periurethral zone of prostate.

questions.answerText: Prostatic venous plexus is located in between the true & false capsule of prostate & presented clinical condition involves periurethral zone of prostate.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Prostatic venous plexus is located in between the true & false capsule of prostate & presented clinical condition involves periurethral zone of prostate

 

The patient’s clinical presentation, combined with the use of Tamsulosin (alpha-blocker) and Finasteride (5-alpha-reductase inhibitor), indicates a diagnosis of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH). This condition involves the periurethral zone of the prostate.

 

In BPH, the enlarged periurethral gland compresses the urethra, causing urinary symptoms like frequency, hesitancy, and urgency.

 

Why TURP is preferred over suprapubic prostatectomy:

 

  • The prostatic venous plexus is located between the true and false capsule of the prostate.
  • A suprapubic prostatectomy requires incising the false capsule, leading to a higher risk of damaging the venous plexus, which can cause severe bleeding and potential complications like shock.
  • In contrast, TURP allows for the removal of only the affected periurethral zone from within the urethra, minimizing damage to the surrounding structures and preserving the venous plexus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Peripheral zone of prostate: Incorrect. BPH primarily affects the periurethral zone, not the peripheral zone. The peripheral zone is typically involved in prostate cancer.

 

Option B. Prostatic venous plexus below the true capsule: Incorrect. The prostatic venous plexus is located between the true and false capsule, not below the true capsule.

 

Option D. Prostatic venous plexus outside the false capsule: Incorrect. The venous plexus lies between the true and false capsules, not outside the false capsule.

 

Educational Objective:

 

TURP is preferred in BPH because it minimizes damage to the prostatic venous plexus (located between the true and false capsule) and allows targeted removal of the periurethral zone, which is the site of enlargement in BPH.

questions.stemHtml: The type of joint marked in the image below is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Synovial


The joint marked in the image is the costovertebral joint, where the rib articulates with the vertebra. The costovertebral joint is classified as a plane synovial joint, characterized by flat articulating surfaces with a small amount of synovial fluid that allows gliding movements. This type of joint provides stability while permitting limited movement necessary for respiration.

 

Key Features of the Costovertebral Joint:

 

  1. Articulating Surfaces: The head of the rib articulates with the superior costal facet of the corresponding thoracic vertebra and the inferior costal facet of the vertebra above.
  2. Joint Capsule: A fibrous capsule lined with synovial membrane surrounds the joint.
  3. Type of Movement: Gliding movements occur at this joint, facilitating rib cage expansion during breathing.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Syndesmosis: Incorrect. Syndesmosis is a fibrous joint where bones are joined by ligaments or interosseous membranes, such as the middle radioulnar joint.

 

Option B. Synarthrosis: Incorrect. Synarthrosis refers to immovable joints, such as sutures of the skull.

 

Option C. Synchondrosis: Incorrect. Synchondrosis is a cartilaginous joint, such as the epiphyseal plate in growing bones.

 

Educational Objective:


The costovertebral joint is a plane synovial joint, allowing gliding movements essential for respiratory function.

questions.stem: The movements at the_________joint permit a person to look to the right and left?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Atlanto-axial


The atlanto-axial joint is a pivot joint, allowing rotational movement. This is the joint responsible for the side-to-side 'no' motion of the head. Pivot joints permit rotation around a single axis, and this feature is essential for head and neck mobility. Other examples of pivot joints include:

 

  • Superior radioulnar joint (at the elbow)
  • Inferior radioulnar joint (at the wrist)

 

Distinction Between Atlanto-axial and Atlanto-occipital Joints:

 

  • The atlanto-axial joint facilitates the 'no' motion (rotation) of the head.
  • The atlanto-occipital joint, located between the atlas (C1) and the occipital bone, allows the 'yes' motion (flexion and extension) and is classified as an ellipsoid joint.

 

Educational Objective:
 

The atlanto-axial joint is a pivot joint responsible for the rotational ('no') motion of the head, while the atlanto-occipital joint is an ellipsoid joint that enables the flexion/extension ('yes') motion.

questions.stem: Cholecystocaval line is in between?

options.label: D
options.text: It is anatomical demarcation between right and left lobe of liver

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Gall bladder & IVC

 

The Cholecystocaval line, also known as Cantlie’s line, is an imaginary line drawn between the gallbladder and the inferior vena cava (IVC). It is significant in liver surgeries as it represents the true midline of the liver, dividing the liver into functional right and left lobes. This is important because:

 

  1. Anatomical midline (ligamentum falciforme and other ligaments): Anatomical divisions of the liver (right and left lobes) are based on surface landmarks like the ligamentum falciforme and ligamentum teres anteriorly, or ligamentum venosum posteriorly. However, these landmarks do not correspond to the liver’s functional division.
  2. Surgical significance: For surgical procedures, the Cholecystocaval line is preferred as it more accurately reflects the division of the liver based on blood supply, bile drainage, and segmental anatomy.

 

This line extends from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Caudate and quadrate lobe: These are lobes of the liver located in close proximity but are not involved in the definition of the Cholecystocaval line.

 

Option B. Caudate lobe and IVC: While the caudate lobe lies near the IVC, the Cholecystocaval line does not demarcate these two structures.

 

Option D. Anatomical demarcation between right and left lobe of liver: While it may act as a functional surgical midline, the Cholecystocaval line is not the anatomical demarcation, which is based on ligamentum falciforme and ligamentum teres.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Cholecystocaval line (Cantlie’s line) is an imaginary line passing between the gallbladder and the IVC, representing the functional midline of the liver used in surgical procedures.

questions.stem: Vitamin A storing liver cell is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ito cells

 

Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin stored primarily in the liver, where specialized cells called Ito cells, also known as hepatic stellate cells, serve as the storage site. Here’s the detailed process:

 

 

  1. Ito cells are located in the space of Disse, the area between the hepatocyte and the sinusoidal endothelial lining.
  2. They are characterized by their star-shaped morphology (stellate appearance).
  3. These cells store vitamin A in the form of lipid droplets.
  4. In cases of vitamin A deficiency, clinical signs such as Bitot’s spots, xerophthalmia, and nyctalopia (night blindness) can occur.
  5.  Ito cells are also known as Stellate cells.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Kupffer cells: These are resident macrophages of the liver located within the sinusoids. They play a role in phagocytosis and immune response but do not store vitamin A.

 

Option C. Hepatocytes: These are the main functional cells of the liver responsible for metabolism, protein synthesis, and detoxification. While they play a role in bile production and nutrient processing, they are not the primary site for vitamin A storage.

 

Option D. Mallory bodies: These are cytoplasmic inclusions found in hepatocytes, often associated with alcoholic liver disease. They have no role in vitamin A storage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ito cells (hepatic stellate cells) in the space of Disse are responsible for storing vitamin A in the liver. They play a critical role in maintaining vitamin A reserves and overall liver health.

questions.stem: Incudostapedial joint is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ball & Socket

 

The incudostapedial joint is a small synovial joint located between the incus (anvil) and the stapes (stirrup) in the middle ear. It facilitates the transmission of sound vibrations from the middle ear to the inner ear. Here's why it is classified as a ball and socket joint:

 

 

  1. Structure: The stapes has a ball-like structure that fits into a corresponding socket on the incus.
  2. Movement: This configuration allows for the necessary rotational movement to transmit sound effectively through the ossicular chain.

 

The joint's design is critical for the mechanical function of the auditory system.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pivot: A pivot joint allows for rotational movement around a single axis (e.g., atlanto-axial joint in the neck). This does not apply to the incudostapedial joint.

 

Option B. Saddle: A saddle joint is characterized by reciprocal concave and convex surfaces (e.g., carpometacarpal joint of the thumb). This applies to the malleoincudal joint, not the incudostapedial joint.

 

Option C. Hinge: Hinge joints allow movement in one plane (e.g., elbow joint). This is not applicable to the incudostapedial joint.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The incudostapedial joint is a ball and socket joint, facilitating precise movement required for the effective transmission of sound waves in the middle ear.

questions.stemHtml: In femoral hernia surgery it is very important to give proper incisions. To increase diameter of femoral canal, we have to cut lacunar ligament & protect the inguinal & pectineal ligaments. Identify the ligaments in image?

options.label: A
options.text: A-Inguinal ligament, B-lacunar ligament, C-Pectineal ligament

options.label: B
options.text: A-Lacunar ligament, B-Inguinal ligament, C-Pectineal ligament

options.label: C
options.text: A-Pectineal ligament, B-Inguinal ligament, C-Lacunar ligament

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) A-Inguinal ligament,B-Pectineal ligament, C-Lacunar ligament

 

In the provided image, we can observe three important ligaments involved in the anatomy of the femoral canal:

 

  • Inguinal ligament (A):
    • This ligament is a modification of the external oblique aponeurosis and runs from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle. It forms the anterior boundary of the femoral canal.
  • Pectineal ligament (B):
    • Also called the Cooper’s ligament, it lies along the pecten pubis (pectineal line of the pubis). It forms the posterior boundary of the femoral canal and provides structural support.
  • Lacunar ligament (C):
    • A crescent-shaped ligament located medially at the femoral canal. Cutting this ligament is crucial during femoral hernia surgery to expand the canal for reducing the hernia.

 

Clinical Importance:


In femoral hernia surgeries, the lacunar ligament is cut to enlarge the femoral canal while preserving the inguinal ligament (to maintain the structural integrity of the groin) and the pectineal ligament.

 

The femoral sheath contains three compartments:

 

  • Medial compartment: Contains femoral lymph nodes.
  • Intermediate compartment: Contains the femoral vein.
  • Lateral compartment: Contains the femoral artery.

 

Important boundaries of the femoral canal:

 

  • Lacunar ligament (medial boundary).
  • Inguinal ligament (anterior boundary).
  • Femoral vein (lateral boundary).
  • Pectineal ligament (posterior boundary).

 

Mnemonic for external oblique muscle modifications: LIP

 

L: Lacunar ligament

 

I: Inguinal ligament

 

P: Pectineal ligament

 

Educational Objective:

 

In femoral hernia surgeries:

 

  • Lacunar ligament is cut to expand the femoral canal.
  • Inguinal ligament and pectineal ligament must be protected.
    The mnemonic LIP (Lacunar, Inguinal, Pectineal) helps recall the ligaments related to femoral hernias.

questions.stemHtml: Greater & lesser sciatic notches are important part of hip bone. These notches act like gateway for pelvic cavity through which many important structures passes. In between these 2 notches one important bony landmark is located as marked in image. Which procedure is related with indicated area?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pudendal nerve block

 

The bony landmark indicated in the image is the ischial spine, located between the greater sciatic notch and the lesser sciatic notch. The ischial spine is a key anatomical structure as several important neurovascular structures pass nearby, including the pudendal nerve, internal pudendal artery, and nerve to obturator internus.

 

The pudendal nerve block is a common gynecological and obstetrical procedure performed to provide local anesthesia to the perineal region. During this procedure, the ischial spine is palpated through vaginal or rectal examination, and the pudendal nerve is anesthetized to block sensation in the perineum.

 

Key Details:

 

  • Structures passing over the ischial spine:
    • P: Pudendal nerve
    • I: Internal pudendal artery
    • N: Nerve to obturator internus
      Mnemonic: PIN
  • Clinical importance:
    • Pudendal nerve block is performed in procedures involving the lower genital tract, vaginal deliveries, and rectal surgeries to provide pain relief or anesthesia.
  • Root value of the pudendal nerve:
    • S2, S3, S4 (mnemonic: "S2, 3, 4 keeps the pelvic floor").

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Pringle’s Maneuver: This is a procedure performed during hepatic surgeries to control bleeding by occluding the portal triad (hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct). It is unrelated to the ischial spine.

 

Option C. Murphy’s Punch biopsy test: This is a clinical test for kidney tenderness during suspected pyelonephritis. It is unrelated to the hip bone or ischial spine.

 

Option D. Murphy’s triad: Refers to the clinical symptoms of acute cholecystitis (right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis) and is unrelated to the ischial spine.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The ischial spine is the key landmark for performing a pudendal nerve block, which is commonly used in perineal procedures to anesthetize the pudendal nerve.

Educational Objective: The ischial spine is the key landmark for performing a pudendal nerve block, which is commonly used in perineal procedures to anesthetize the pudendal nerve.

questions.stemHtml: Which structure doesn’t contract in case of diaphragmatic constriction:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A

 

In the context of diaphragmatic contraction, A (Inferior Vena Cava) does not contract due to its location within the central tendon of the diaphragm. The central tendon is a non-contractile structure, which means it does not exhibit muscular contraction. Instead, when the diaphragm contracts, the central tendon stretches and expands, which increases the diameter of the inferior vena cava (IVC). This expansion aids in venous return by facilitating the flow of blood through the IVC.

 

 

 

Key Features:

 

  • Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) passes through the central tendon at the T8 vertebral level.
  • The central tendon is a connective tissue structure that does not contract.
  • As the diaphragm contracts, the IVC opening widens, promoting increased venous return to the heart.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. B (Esophagus): The esophageal opening is surrounded by muscular fibers of the diaphragm. When the diaphragm contracts, these fibers tighten, compressing the esophagus to prevent reflux.

 

Option C. C (Aorta): The aorta passes through the aortic hiatus, which lies posterior to the diaphragm. While the aortic wall itself does not contract, the surrounding muscular activity and pressure changes indirectly affect the aorta.

 

Additional information:

 

 Diaphragms in the body:

 

  1. Diaphragma sellae: Separates the pituitary gland from the cranial cavity.
  2. Iris: Separates the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye.
  3. Mylohyoid muscle: Forms a diaphragm between the mouth and neck.
  4. Sibson’s fascia: Diaphragm between the neck and thoracic cavity (suprapleural membrane).
  5. Thoracoabdominal diaphragm: Primary diaphragm separating thoracic and abdominal cavities.
  6. Pelvic diaphragm: Separates abdominal cavity from the pelvic cavity.
  7. Urogenital diaphragm: Found in the perineum.
  8. Femoral sheath septa: Acts as a diaphragm-like structure in the femoral triangle.

 

Thoracoabdominal diaphragm openings and levels:

 

  • Inferior vena cava (IVC): At T8, mnemonic: VENA CAVA has 8 letters. Structures passing through:
    • Inferior vena cava
    • Right phrenic nerve
  • Esophagus: At T10, mnemonic: ESOPHAGUS has 10 letters. Structures passing through:
    • Esophagus
    • Left and right vagus nerves
    • Left gastric vessels
  • Aorta: At T12, mnemonic: AORTIC HIATUS has 12 letters. Structures passing through:
    • Aorta
    • Thoracic duct
    • Azygos vein
  • Mnemonics:
    • V = I × R: IVC (Inferior vena cava + Right phrenic nerve).
    • LOVE: Left gastric vessels, vagus nerve, esophagus.

questions.stem: Harris dictum is related to which viscera:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Spleen

 

Harris dictum is a set of measurements and anatomical details related to the spleen, emphasizing its odd dimensions, weight, and location. This mnemonic makes it easy to recall the key features of the spleen:

 

  1. Odd Dimensions:
    • Thickness: 1 inch
    • Width: 3 inches
    • Length: 5 inches
  2. Weight:
    • Approximately 1 ounce (or about 150 grams).
  3. Location:
    • The spleen lies under the 9th to 11th ribs on the left side of the body.

 

These dimensions and relationships were summarized and popularized by Harris, hence the term Harris dictum.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pancreas: Harris dictum is not related to the pancreas, which has different anatomical and clinical details.

 

Option B. Liver: The liver has its own clinical mnemonics and anatomical descriptions, such as Couinaud segments, not Harris dictum.

 

Option C. Kidney: Kidneys are measured and located differently, unrelated to Harris dictum.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Harris dictum summarizes the odd measurements, weight, and location of the spleen, helping in its anatomical and clinical understanding.

questions.stem: A 13 years old male Sulabh, presented with pain in right iliac fossa, vomiting & fever. On blood examination leucocytosis was found in this patient point of maximum tenderness is?

options.label: A
options.text: Junction between lateral 2/3rd & medial 1/3rd between umblico- spinal line

options.label: B
options.text: Junction between medial 2/3rd & lateral 1/3rd between umblico- spinal line

options.label: C
options.text: Junction between lateral 3/5th & medial 2/5th between umblico- spinal line

options.label: D
options.text: Junction between lateral 2/5th & medial 3/5th between umblico- spinal line

questions.answerText: Junction between medial 2/3rd & lateral 1/3rd between umblico- spinal line
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Junction between medial 2/3rd & lateral 1/3rd between umblico- spinal line

 

The symptoms of pain in the right iliac fossa, vomiting, fever, and leucocytosis strongly suggest acute appendicitis, a condition diagnosed based on Murphy’s triad (pain, vomiting, fever).

 

The point of maximum tenderness in appendicitis is typically located at McBurney’s point, which is the junction between the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third of a line drawn between the umbilicus and anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS). This line is referred to as the spino-umbilical line.

 

 

Clinical Importance of McBurney's Point:

 

  • It is used to localize pain and tenderness in cases of appendicitis.
  • Inflammation of the appendix typically irritates the parietal peritoneum, causing sharp pain at this location.

 

Differential diagnoses include other causes of right lower quadrant pain such as mesenteric adenitis, Meckel’s diverticulitis, or gynecological conditions in females.

 

Note:

 

Murphy's terms to remember:

 

  • Murphy's Triad: Associated with acute appendicitis.
  • Murphy's Sign: Used in diagnosing acute cholecystitis (pain on inspiration during right upper quadrant palpation).
  • Murphy's Eye: Pediatric relevance (endotracheal tube feature).
  • Murphy's Punch Test: Renal biopsy or tenderness over the costovertebral angle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Junction between lateral 2/3rd & medial 1/3rd of the umbilico-spinal line: This point does not correspond to McBurney’s point and is anatomically inaccurate for appendicitis.

 

Option C. Junction between lateral 3/5th & medial 2/5th of the umbilico-spinal line: This is not a recognized location associated with appendicitis.

 

Option D. Junction between lateral 2/5th & medial 3/5th of the umbilico-spinal line: This is also incorrect and not related to McBurney’s point.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The maximum tenderness in acute appendicitis is typically felt at McBurney’s point, located at the junction between the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third of the line between the umbilicus and anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).

questions.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman was admitted in the emergency room with severe epigastric pain with radiation to the back, nausea, anorexia, jaundice, 38.5 ºC fever, headache and myalgia. Examination revealed a woman with severe jaundice, pallor, and epigastric abdominal pain during superficial palpation, with no peritonitis signs. Her liver was enlarged, exceeding costal margin by 2 cm. Laboratory investigations showed serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 1,285 IU/L (13-35 IU/dL), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 666 IU/L (7-35 IU/dL), lipase 1,012 IU/L (≤ 200 IU/L), amylase 149 IU/L (20-110UI/L). She was diagnosed with acute pancreatitis. In this case which arterial aneurism may be seen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Splenic artery

 

In acute pancreatitis, the pancreas undergoes autodigestion due to the activation of digestive enzymes within the gland. This process, particularly when severe, can involve surrounding tissues, including blood vessels. The splenic artery, which runs along the upper border of the pancreas, is the most commonly affected artery due to its proximity to the inflamed pancreas.

 

Mechanism of Splenic Artery Involvement:

 

  1. Autodigestion of Pancreas: Release of enzymes like elastase and lipase results in the destruction of nearby tissues, including the arterial walls.
  2. Splenic Artery Proximity: The splenic artery is directly adjacent to the pancreas, making it highly susceptible to enzymatic damage.
  3. Formation of Aneurysm: Damage to the arterial wall weakens it, leading to the formation of an aneurysm.
  4. (Aneurysm is formation of bulge or ballooning in the vessel wall due to weakness in the vessel wall).
  5. Due to autodigestion of pancreas the splenic artery which is in close relation to the pancreas also gets affected. Weakness in the vessel wall takes place which leads to formation of aneurysm.  

 

Key Clinical Features:

 

 

  • Cullen’s Sign: Hemorrhage around the umbilicus (as shown in the image).
  • Grey-Turner’s Sign: Hemorrhage in the flank region.
  • Both signs indicate retroperitoneal hemorrhage, often seen in severe pancreatitis.

 

Supporting Data:

 

  • Elevated AST and ALT: Indicate liver involvement, likely due to biliary pancreatitis (e.g., gallstones).
  • Elevated lipase and amylase: Confirm acute pancreatitis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Superior pancreatico-duodenal artery: This artery supplies the head of the pancreas but is less commonly affected compared to the splenic artery.

 

Option B. Inferior pancreatico-duodenal artery: Supplies part of the pancreas but is rarely involved in aneurysm formation during acute pancreatitis.

 

Option D. Arteria pancreatica magna: A branch supplying the body of the pancreas but is not the most common site for aneurysms in pancreatitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In acute pancreatitis, the most common arterial aneurysm occurs in the splenic artery due to its anatomical proximity and exposure to digestive enzymes. The presence of Cullen’s and Grey-Turner’s signs suggests severe pancreatitis with retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

questions.stemHtml: Fascia shown in image is known as------- & it is attached to------------- vertebra:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Diaphragm of neck; C7

 

The fascia shown in the image is Sibson’s fascia, also known as the suprapleural membrane. It is a tough fibrous layer that acts as a diaphragm of the neck, separating the thoracic cavity from the neck. This fascia:

 

  • Covers the apex of the lung and the pleura above it.
  • Is attached laterally to the inner border of the first rib and medially to the transverse process of the C7 vertebra.

 

 

Key Features:

 

  • Location and Role:
    • Protects the apex of the lung and its pleura.
    • Prevents the lung from herniating into the neck.
  • Attachments:
    • Lateral attachment: Inner border of the first rib.
    • Medial attachment: Transverse process of C7 vertebra.
  • Structure:
    • It is a continuation of the endothoracic fascia, strengthened by tendinous fibers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Diaphragm of mouth; C1: Incorrect. The diaphragm of the mouth is mylohyoid muscle, and it is not attached to the C1 vertebra.

 

Option B. Diaphragm of mouth; C2: Incorrect. Same as above; the diaphragm of the mouth does not attach to C2.

 

Option C. Diaphragm of neck; C6: Incorrect. The Sibson’s fascia is attached to C7, not C6.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sibson’s fascia (suprapleural membrane) is the diaphragm of the neck, separating the thorax and neck and attached medially to the transverse process of C7 vertebra.

questions.stem: Extra rib present above 1st rib and below 12th rib are known as:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cervical rib & Gorilla rib

 

  • Cervical rib:
    • An extra rib above the 1st rib, arising from the C7 vertebra, is called a cervical rib.
    • It occurs in 0.5-1% of the population and can cause thoracic outlet syndrome by compressing nearby structures like the brachial plexus or subclavian artery.
  • Gorilla rib:
    • An extra rib below the 12th rib, also known as the 13th rib, is commonly seen in gorillas and other primates but is rare in humans.
    • This is also referred to as a lumbar rib or gorilla rib and may not have clinical significance unless it causes mechanical problems.
    • Ribs are classified with respect to their attachment at the anterior end. Rib 1 to 7 are directly attached with sternum and are classified as true ribs. Rib number 8 to 10 are attached with sternum by the help of cartilage. Such ribs are classified as false ribs. RIb number 11 and below are classified as floating ribs since they are free at their anterior end. 
    • The extra rib below 12th is a type of floating rib and it is called Gorilla rib or lumbar rib.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cervical rib & Floating rib: Floating ribs (11th and 12th ribs) are normal anatomical structures, not extra ribs.

 

Option C. Cervical rib & Renal rib: "Renal rib" is not a recognized term in anatomical or clinical practice.

 

Option D. Supra rib & Cervical rib: "Supra rib" is not a recognized term in anatomy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Extra ribs in humans include:

 

  • Cervical rib: Extra rib above the 1st rib (C7 vertebra).
  • Gorilla rib: Extra rib below the 12th rib, resembling the 13th rib in primates.

questions.stemHtml: In shown image one important structure is present which is joined to 3 systems of body during embryonic period (CVS, GIT & Excretory system). What is the vertebral level of this embryonic structure:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) L3 – L4

 

The structure referenced in the question is the umbilicus, a critical landmark in human anatomy. During the embryonic period, the umbilicus is connected to three systems of the body:

 

  1. Cardiovascular system (CVS): Via the umbilical arteries and veins, which supply and return blood between the fetus and placenta.
  2. Gastrointestinal system (GIT): Through the vitelline duct, connecting the midgut to the yolk sac.
  3. Excretory system: Through the urachus (a remnant of the allantois), which connects the fetal bladder to the umbilicus.

 

The vertebral level of the umbilicus is at L3–L4, which is also a significant clinical landmark:

 

  • It helps locate the transumbilical plane, dividing the upper and lower abdomen.
  • It is the level where the aorta bifurcates into the common iliac arteries.
  • In adults, this is a useful landmark for lumbar puncture procedures, identified with the help of the iliac crests.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. L1 – L2: Incorrect. This level corresponds to the transpyloric plane, unrelated to the umbilicus.

 

Option B. L2 – L3: Incorrect. This is not the precise vertebral level of the umbilicus.

 

Option D. L4 – L5: Incorrect. This level corresponds to the trans-tubercular plane, which is below the umbilicus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The umbilicus is located at the vertebral level of L3–L4, serving as a key anatomical landmark during development and in clinical practice.

questions.stem: A man was brought to the emergency department after he fell into a manhole and injured his perineum. He was unable to pass urine and blood was seen at the tip of the urethra. A diagnosis of bulbar urethral injury was made. Where do you least expect the urine to get collected in this case?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Medial portion of thigh

 

A bulbar urethral injury typically leads to extravasation of urine and blood into spaces defined by the anatomy of the perineum and anterior abdominal wall.

 

  • The bulbar urethra is located in the superficial perineal space, and any rupture here results in urine escaping into the surrounding connective tissue spaces.
  • From the perineum, urine can track into the penile shaft, scrotum, and anterior abdominal wall due to the continuity of the superficial fascia in these regions (Colles’ fascia in the perineum, Dartos fascia in the scrotum, and Scarpa’s fascia in the anterior abdominal wall).
  • However, urine cannot enter the medial portion of the thigh because the fascia lata of the thigh creates a boundary that prevents the spread of urine into this area.

 

Key Points About Urethral Injury:

 

  1. Causes: Commonly caused by blunt perineal trauma, such as falling onto a hard surface (e.g., a manhole).
  2. Symptoms: Inability to void urine, blood at the external urethral meatus, and swelling of the perineum or scrotum.
  3. Diagnosis: Clinical examination and retrograde urethrography are typically used to confirm the injury.

 

 

Four parts of the urethra :

 

  • Prostatic urethra
  • Membranous urethra
  • Bulbar urethra
  • Penile (spongy) urethra

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Perineum: Incorrect. Urine commonly collects in the perineum in bulbar urethral injuries.

 

Option B. Anterior abdominal wall: Incorrect. Urine can track into the anterior abdominal wall due to the continuity of the superficial fascia.

 

Option D. Root of scrotum: Incorrect. Urine frequently collects in the scrotum following bulbar urethral injury.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of bulbar urethral injury, urine extravasates into the perineum, scrotum, and anterior abdominal wall but does not collect in the medial portion of the thigh due to the restrictive boundary of the fascia lata.

questions.stemHtml: This type of tissue is found in?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ureter

 

The image shows transitional epithelium, also known as urothelium, which is a specialized epithelial tissue found in the urinary tract, including the ureters, urinary bladder, and renal pelvis. This epithelium is adapted to stretch and accommodate the fluctuating volumes of urine.

 

Key Features of Transitional Epithelium:

 

  1. Multiple layers: It appears stratified, with three distinct layers:
    • Basal cells: Located near the basement membrane, these are cuboidal in shape.
    • Intermediate cells: These are pear-shaped (broad above and narrow below).
    • Superficial (umbrella) cells: The large surface cells often have a characteristic dome or umbrella shape, with internalized membrane structures to allow for distension.
  2. Binucleation: Some of the umbrella cells may show two nuclei.
  3. Internalization of the cell membrane: This allows the cells to expand when the organ stretches.

 

Location of Transitional Epithelium:

 

  • Found in the urinary tract, including:
    • Renal pelvis
    • Ureter
    • Urinary bladder
    • Proximal urethra

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Heart: Incorrect. The heart is lined by simple squamous epithelium (endothelium), not transitional epithelium.

 

Option B. Female genital tract: Incorrect. The female genital tract has columnar or squamous epithelium, depending on the region, but no transitional epithelium.

 

Option C. Trachea: Incorrect. The trachea is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with cilia, not transitional epithelium.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Transitional epithelium is characteristic of the urinary tract, particularly the ureters, urinary bladder, and renal pelvis, allowing these organs to stretch and return to their normal size.

questions.stem: Neurovascular bundle of thoracic & abdominal cavity runs in between the:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Middle and inner layers

 

The neurovascular bundle, consisting of the vein, artery, and nerve (VAN), is located between the middle layer (internal oblique muscle in the abdomen or internal intercostal muscle in the thorax) and the innermost layer (innermost intercostal muscle in the thorax or transversus abdominis in the abdomen). This arrangement provides protection and facilitates the functional organization of these structures within the body wall.

 

In the thorax, the neurovascular bundle is located in the costal groove of the ribs, which provides a specific path for these vessels and nerves. The relationship of the VAN is critical during procedures such as thoracocentesis to avoid injury.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Outer and middle layers: Incorrect. The outer layer is the external oblique or external intercostal muscle, and the neurovascular bundle does not run between this and the middle layer.

 

Option C. Outer and inner layers: Incorrect. The neurovascular bundle does not traverse directly between the outermost and innermost layers; it is specifically located between the middle and inner layers.

 

Option D. None: Incorrect. The neurovascular bundle clearly has a defined location between the middle and inner layers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The neurovascular bundle (VAN) of the thoracic and abdominal cavity runs between the middle layer (internal oblique/internal intercostal) and the innermost layer (innermost intercostal/transversus abdominis). Always remember this relationship to avoid damage during procedures like thoracocentesis.

questions.stemHtml: Identify vertebra:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) A-Cervical, B- Thoracic, C- Lumbar


To identify vertebrae, it is essential to note key distinguishing features:

 

  • Cervical vertebra (A): The presence of a transverse foramen (foramen transversarium) is a hallmark feature of cervical vertebrae. These foramina allow the passage of the vertebral artery. This characteristic is clearly observed in vertebra A in the image.
  • Thoracic vertebra (B): Thoracic vertebrae have a long, downward-pointing spinous process and costal facets that articulate with the ribs. These features are evident in vertebra B.
  • Lumbar vertebra (C): Lumbar vertebrae are characterized by their large, robust bodies (to bear weight) and short, blunt spinous processes. The vertebral canal is triangular in shape. These features are present in vertebra C.

 

Educational Objective:
 

To identify vertebrae:

 

  1. Cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina (foramen transversarium).
  2. Thoracic vertebrae have long spines and costal facets for rib articulation.
  3. Lumbar vertebrae have large bodies, short spines, and triangular vertebral canals.

The image represents the anterior abdominal wall muscles and associated structures. Identifying these structures:

 

  • I - Linea alba: This is the midline raphe formed by the aponeuroses of the abdominal muscles. It is a prominent central structure.
  • II - Linea semilunaris: This semilunar-shaped structure marks the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis muscle.

The external oblique muscle of the anterior abdominal wall is characterized by the linea alba (midline), linea semilunaris (lateral edge of rectus abdominis), inguinal ligament (lower free edge), and insertion on the outer lip of the iliac crest.

questions.stemHtml: During hepatobiliary surgery indicated procedure as shown image was performed to prevent bleeding and biliary leakage. In this procedure the index finger is inserted along free margin of lesser omentum. It is done at which vertebral level:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) T12


The procedure demonstrated in the image is known as Pringle’s maneuver, which involves clamping the structures within the hepatoduodenal ligament to control bleeding and prevent bile leakage during hepatobiliary surgery. The hepatoduodenal ligament is the free edge of the lesser omentum and contains the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct (VAD structures). The maneuver involves inserting the index finger through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), which connects the greater sac to the lesser sac.

 

The vertebral level associated with the epiploic foramen is T12, located just above the first part of the duodenum (D1), which lies at the L1 level.

 

 

Boundaries of the epiploic foramen:

 

  1. Superior boundary: Liver
  2. Inferior boundary: First part of the duodenum (D1)
  3. Anterior boundary: Portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct (VAD structures)
  4. Posterior boundary: Inferior vena cava (IVC) and right crus of the diaphragm

 

This vertebral level (T12) is critical for anatomical orientation during surgical procedures involving the hepatoduodenal ligament.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. T11: Incorrect, as the epiploic foramen lies below this level. T11 corresponds to regions higher in the abdominal cavity.

 

Option C. L1: Incorrect, as L1 marks the level of the first part of the duodenum (D1), which is inferior to the epiploic foramen.

 

Option D. L2: Incorrect, as L2 is associated with the second part of the duodenum (D2), which is lower in the abdominal cavity.

 

Educational Objective:
 

The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), through which the index finger passes during Pringle’s maneuver, is located at the T12 vertebral level. This anatomical knowledge is crucial during hepatobiliary surgeries to avoid complications.

questions.stem: Which of the following are branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery? 1. Superior gluteal artery2. Inferior gluteal artery3. Superior vesical artery4. Middle rectal artery5. Inferior vesical artery6. Vaginal artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 2, 3, 4, 5, 6


The internal iliac artery divides into two major divisions: anterior and posterior. The anterior division supplies most of the pelvic viscera and the perineum, while the posterior division primarily supplies the posterior structures and gluteal region.

 

Branches of the anterior division:

 

  1. Inferior gluteal artery: Supplies the gluteal region and is a major branch of the anterior division.
  2. Superior vesical artery: Supplies the superior part of the bladder and ductus deferens (in males).
  3. Middle rectal artery: Supplies the rectum and anastomoses with other rectal arteries.
  4. Inferior vesical artery (in males): Supplies the inferior part of the bladder, prostate, and seminal vesicles.
    • In females, the equivalent branch is the vaginal artery, which supplies the vagina and adjacent structures.

 

 

Posterior division branches mnemonic: "I love SRK":

 

  • I: Ilio-lumbar artery
  • L: Lateral sacral artery
  • S: Superior gluteal artery

 

The superior gluteal artery is therefore a branch of the posterior division, not the anterior division.

 

Educational Objective:


The anterior division of the internal iliac artery provides branches that predominantly supply the pelvic viscera, including the inferior gluteal artery, superior vesical artery, middle rectal artery, inferior vesical artery (males), and vaginal artery (females).

questions.stem: Middle colic artery is branch of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Superior mesenteric artery 


The middle colic artery is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). The superior mesenteric artery is responsible for supplying the midgut, which includes the pancreas, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, ascending colon, and transverse colon. Specifically, the middle colic artery supplies the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.

 

 

The vascular supply of the gastrointestinal tract is organized as follows:

 

  1. Foregut: Supplied by the celiac trunk, which has three branches:
    • Left gastric artery
    • Splenic artery
    • Common hepatic artery
  2. Midgut: Supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), which has six branches:
    • Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery
    • Jejunal and ileal arteries
    • Ileocolic artery
    • Right colic artery
    • Middle colic artery
  3. Hindgut: Supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), which has three branches:
    • Left colic artery
    • Sigmoid artery
    • Superior rectal artery

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Celiac trunk: Incorrect, as this supplies the foregut, not the midgut.

 

Option C. Inferior mesenteric artery: Incorrect, as this supplies the hindgut (e.g., descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum).

 

Option D. Ileocolic artery: Incorrect, as this is another branch of the superior mesenteric artery but supplies the cecum and appendix, not the transverse colon.

 

Educational Objective:


The middle colic artery, which supplies the transverse colon, is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA).

questions.stem: A tumor of the uncinate process of the pancreas affects which of the following vessels?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Superior mesenteric artery


The uncinate process of the pancreas is a small projection from the head of the pancreas that lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels (both the superior mesenteric artery and vein). A tumor in this region can compress the superior mesenteric vessels, leading to vascular complications.

 

 

Key anatomical relations of the uncinate process:

 

  1. The superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein) pass anterior to the uncinate process.
  2. The splenic vein, coming from the spleen, joins with the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.

 

While the superior mesenteric artery is directly affected due to its anterior relation to the uncinate process, the portal vein is less likely to be directly compressed. The common hepatic artery and inferior mesenteric artery are located farther away and are not associated with the uncinate process.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Portal vein: Incorrect, as the portal vein is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein but is not directly compressed by tumors in the uncinate process.

 

Option C. Common hepatic artery: Incorrect, as this artery is a branch of the celiac trunk and is not located near the uncinate process.

 

Option D. Inferior mesenteric artery: Incorrect, as this artery supplies the hindgut and is far from the pancreas.

 

Educational Objective:
 

A tumor in the uncinate process of the pancreas commonly compresses the superior mesenteric artery and vein due to their close anatomical relationship.

questions.stem: Brain and spinal cord develops from:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Neuroectoderm

 

The brain and spinal cord develop from the neuroectoderm, a specialized part of the ectoderm. During embryological development:

 

  1. The ectoderm differentiates into two major components:
    • Surface ectoderm: Forms structures like the epidermis, hair, and nails.
    • Neuroectoderm: Develops into the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS).
  2. The neuroectoderm forms a neural plate, which undergoes a series of transformations:
    • The neural plate folds to form the neural groove.
    • The groove then closes to form the neural tube.
    • The neural tube shows cranial dilation (forming the brain) and caudal narrowing (forming the spinal cord).

 

Thus, the neuroectoderm gives rise to both the brain and spinal cord.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ectoderm: While the neuroectoderm originates from the ectoderm, the term "ectoderm" is too broad and includes surface ectoderm as well, which is unrelated to brain and spinal cord formation. Hence, it is not the best answer.

 

Option C. Neural crest cells: These cells arise from the edges of the neural tube and form structures such as peripheral nerves, adrenal medulla, and facial cartilage but do not directly form the brain or spinal cord.

 

Option D. Mesoderm: The mesoderm forms other structures such as muscles, bones, and the circulatory system but has no role in forming the brain or spinal cord.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The brain and spinal cord develop from the neuroectoderm, which is a specialized part of the ectoderm. The neuroectoderm forms the neural plate, which gives rise to the neural groove, neural tube, and eventually the CNS.

questions.stem: Which muscle develops from 1st pharyngeal arch?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Anterior belly of digastric

 

The 1st pharyngeal arch contributes to the development of several muscles, primarily those associated with mastication. These muscles are derived from the mandibular nerve (V3), a branch of the trigeminal nerve. The first arch develops a total of eight muscles, grouped into:

 

  1. Muscles of mastication:
    • Temporalis
    • Masseter
    • Medial pterygoid
    • Lateral pterygoid
  2. Other muscles associated with the 1st pharyngeal arch:
    • Mylohyoid (forms the diaphragm of the floor of the mouth)
    • Anterior belly of digastric
    • Tensor tympani
    • Tensor veli palatini

 

The anterior belly of digastric is one of the key muscles derived from the 1st pharyngeal arch. It plays a role in depressing the mandible and elevating the hyoid bone during swallowing and speech.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Posterior belly of digastric: Derived from the 2nd pharyngeal arch, not the 1st. It is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

 

Option C. Stapedius: Developed from the 2nd pharyngeal arch and also supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

 

Option D. Stylohyoid: Also derived from the 2nd pharyngeal arch and supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

 

Educational Objective:

 

The anterior belly of digastric is derived from the 1st pharyngeal arch, along with the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini. These muscles are all innervated by the mandibular nerve (V3).

questions.stemHtml: The following image shows transverse section of spinal cord in the cervical region of human embryo, early in the 6th week of life. Identify the position of the notochord in the image below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C

 

Option C is notochord since lies in the exact midline, ventral (anterior) to the developing neural tube/spinal cord.

 

The notochord is a key embryological structure that lies just ventral (in front of) the developing neural tube (spinal cord). In this transverse section of the cervical region of a 6-week-old embryo:

 

 

  • A represents the dorsal root, which is sensory in function.
  • B represents the ventral root, which is motor in function.
  • C, positioned ventral to the neural tube, is the notochord, which serves as a temporary axial support structure and plays a critical role in signaling during the development of the neural tube and vertebral column.
  • D represents the developing body wall mesodermal structures.

 

The notochord disappears later in development and its remnants form the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.

 

Developmental Significance of the Notochord:

 

  • It induces the formation of the neural plate from ectoderm.
  • The notochord also stimulates the differentiation of the surrounding mesoderm into the vertebral column components.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The notochord is positioned ventral to the neural tube in the developing embryo and serves as the foundation for the vertebral column and the signaling center for early neural and skeletal development.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following Clinical condition may be seen in tissue shown in image:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cardiomyopathy

 

The histological image shows cardiac muscle tissue, which can be identified by the presence of intercalated discs, branching muscle fibers, and centrally located nuclei. Intercalated discs are unique to cardiac muscle tissue and facilitate synchronized contraction of the heart. 

 

 

Cardiomyopathy is a clinical condition associated with the dysfunction of cardiac muscle, often resulting from genetic mutations, ischemia, or other systemic conditions. The image highlights structural features of cardiac muscle that are key in diagnosing conditions like cardiomyopathy.

 

Cardiomyopathy affects the structure and function of cardiac muscles, leading to abnormalities such as hypertrophy or dilatation of the heart chambers. The histology of affected tissue often reveals disarrangement of fibers and signs of necrosis in advanced stages.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Myasthenia gravis: This condition primarily affects neuromuscular junctions and is associated with skeletal muscle weakness. It does not involve cardiac muscle directly and hence is not related to the tissue shown in the image.

 

Option C. Lambert-Eaton syndrome: This syndrome involves autoimmunity against voltage-gated calcium channels at the neuromuscular junction, also affecting skeletal muscles. It does not involve cardiac muscle histology.

 

Option D. Myotonic dystrophica: Myotonic dystrophy affects skeletal muscles, causing muscle wasting and weakness. It does not involve the characteristic intercalated discs or branching pattern of cardiac muscle tissue seen in the image.

 

Note:

 

  • Rheumatic heart disease is associated with fibrinoid necrosis in cardiac tissue.
  • Key features to observe in histology for rheumatic heart disease:

 

Aschoff bodies

 

Anitschkow cells (with "owl's eye" appearance)

 

Caterpillar nucleus

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cardiac muscle tissue is identified by its branching fibers, centrally located nuclei, and intercalated discs. These features are crucial in understanding conditions such as cardiomyopathy, which affects the structure and function of the cardiac muscle.

questions.stemHtml: A 38-week gestational age infant was noted to have thick secretions and difficulty in breathing on the first day of life. An orogastric tube was unable to be passed into the stomach as shown in image. For treatment thoracotomy surgery was decided. Which of the following will be best approach?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Postero-lateral thoracotomy

 

The given clinical scenario and image indicate a case of tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) with associated esophageal atresia. This condition is characterized by an abnormal connection between the trachea and esophagus, often accompanied by failure of the esophagus to form a continuous canal. In this condition, passing an orogastric tube results in coiling in the proximal esophagus, as seen in the X-ray image.

 

Key Anatomical Features:


The esophagus and trachea are located in the posterior mediastinum, with the esophagus lying behind the trachea. Because of this posterior location, the most direct and least invasive surgical approach is the postero-lateral thoracotomy. This approach avoids cutting through the sternum, lungs, or heart, providing easier access to the esophagus and trachea.

 

 

Clinical Relevance:


Postero-lateral thoracotomy minimizes the risk of damaging critical anterior structures, such as the heart and lungs, and provides the surgeon a clear view of the affected area to repair the fistula and atresia effectively.

 

Note:

 

  • The sternal angle of Louis is located at the T4-T5 vertebral junction, marking the division between the superior and inferior mediastinum.
  • The mnemonic VOT helps recall anatomical relations: Vertebra, esophagus, trachea (from back to front).

 

Types of esophageal atresia with TEF:

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anterior thoracotomy: This approach would require cutting through the sternum and anterior mediastinum, encountering unnecessary obstacles such as the heart and lungs. It is not suitable for accessing posterior structures like the esophagus and trachea.

 

Option B. Antero-lateral thoracotomy: While this approach avoids the sternum, it still involves accessing anterior structures, making it less ideal for addressing the posteriorly located esophagus and trachea.

 

Option C. Posterior thoracotomy: Although this approach targets the posterior mediastinum, it risks directly cutting through the vertebral structures. It does not provide adequate lateral exposure needed for such surgeries.

 

Educational Objective:

 

For surgical repair of tracheoesophageal fistula and esophageal atresia, the postero-lateral thoracotomy approach is preferred due to its direct access to the posterior mediastinum while avoiding anterior structures like the heart and lungs

questions.stemHtml: For RFA of AV node following triangle is targeted in clinical. All of the followings are at boundaries of this triangle except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Anterior leaflet of tricuspid valve

 

The triangle being referred to is Koch's triangle, an anatomical landmark in the right atrium used to locate the atrioventricular (AV) node during radiofrequency ablation procedures. 

 

 

This triangle is bounded by three key structures:

 

  • Tendon of Todaro (Subendocardial ridge):
    • A fibrous structure within the right atrium.
    • Forms the superior boundary of Koch's triangle.
  • Opening of the Coronary Sinus:
    • Located at the base of Koch's triangle.
    • The coronary sinus is the main vein of the heart.
  • Septal Leaflet of the Tricuspid Valve:
    • Forms the anterior boundary of Koch's triangle.

 

The Anterior Leaflet of the Tricuspid Valve is not a boundary of Koch's triangle. It is anatomically located further away and does not contribute to the triangle’s boundaries.

 

Clinical Importance:

 

  • Apex of Koch's Triangle:
    • Houses the AV node, the target for ablation procedures in cases of supraventricular tachycardia.
  • Location of SA Node:
    • Located near the junction of the superior vena cava and crista terminalis, not within Koch's triangle.

 

Note:

 

  • Eustachian Valve: Found at the opening of the inferior vena cava.
  • Thebesian Valve: Found at the opening of the coronary sinus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Koch's triangle is an essential anatomical landmark in the right atrium, bounded by:

 

  1. Tendon of Todaro (Subendocardial ridge)
  2. Opening of Coronary Sinus
  3. Septal Leaflet of Tricuspid Valve

 

The Anterior Leaflet of the Tricuspid Valve is not part of this boundary.

questions.stem: During cardiopulmonary surgery there was need to ligate ascending aorta & pulmonary trunk. Where these structures can be ligated at?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Transverse sinus

 

The transverse sinus is a passage located behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, formed by a fold in the pericardium. It allows the ligation or clamping of these great vessels during cardiopulmonary surgeries such as cardiopulmonary bypass.

 

Key Anatomical Features:

 

  1. Location:
    • The transverse sinus lies anterior to the superior vena cava and posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
  2. Clinical Importance:
    • Surgeons can insert a finger or clamp into the transverse sinus to control or isolate the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. This helps in stopping the blood flow to perform surgeries like heart transplantation or repairing congenital heart defects.

 

 

Boundaries:

 

  • Anterior boundary: Ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
  • Posterior boundary: Superior vena cava and left atrium.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Oblique sinus: The oblique sinus is a space behind the left atrium formed by the pericardial reflection. It is not related to ligating the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.

 

Option C. Triangle of Koch: Koch's triangle is an anatomical landmark within the right atrium, used to locate the AV node during ablation. It is unrelated to ligation of great vessels.

 

Option D. Tendon of Todaro: The Tendon of Todaro is a fibrous structure that forms part of Koch's triangle and has no role in ligation of the ascending aorta or pulmonary trunk.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The transverse sinus is the anatomical space used during cardiopulmonary surgeries to ligate or clamp the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, critical for controlling blood flow during procedures.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the marked structure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Heister’s valve

 

The Hister's valve is located in the neck of the gallbladder. It is also referred to as the spiral valve because it is formed by a series of spiral folds in the mucosa of the cystic duct. These folds help maintain the patency of the cystic duct and regulate the flow of bile.

 

Key Features of Gallbladder Anatomy:

 

  1. Parts of the Gallbladder:
    • Fundus: Rounded, distal portion of the gallbladder.
    • Body: Central portion.
    • Neck: Narrow region leading to the cystic duct, containing the Hister's valve.
  2. Hister’s Valve:
    • Not a true valve (pseudo-valve).
    • Prevents over-distension and kinking of the cystic duct.
  3. Hartmann's Pouch:
    • A small pouch in the neck of the gallbladder where stones frequently lodge.

 

Additional Information on Related Valves:

 

  1. Houston Valve:
    • Found in the rectum, these are transverse folds that support the rectal wall.
  2. Gerlach Valve:
    • A fold found in the appendix, also known as the valve of Gerlach.
  3. Pseudo-Valve:
    • Structures like Hister's valve are considered pseudo-valves because they do not have a true valve function.

 

Clinical Significance:

 

  • Hartmann’s Pouch is a common site for gallstones, which can obstruct the cystic duct and lead to cholecystitis.
  • The Hister’s valve can sometimes cause difficulty in cannulating the cystic duct during surgical or diagnostic procedures.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Hister's valve is located in the neck of the gallbladder and helps maintain bile flow through the cystic duct. It is a false valve, and its anatomy is significant for conditions like gallstones in Hartmann’s pouch.

questions.stemHtml: Indicated duct opens into:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Minor duodenal papilla

 

The duct shown in the image is the accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini). This duct drains part of the pancreas separately from the main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung). The minor duodenal papilla is a small elevation on the inner surface of the duodenum where the accessory pancreatic duct empties digestive enzymes into the duodenum.

 

This anatomical feature serves as a secondary route for pancreatic secretions, playing a minor role in the overall drainage system of the pancreas.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Major duodenal papilla: Incorrect. The major duodenal papilla is the opening for the main pancreatic duct and the common bile duct. It is larger and located 2 cm below the minor duodenal papilla.

 

Option C. Ampulla of Vater: Incorrect. The ampulla of Vater is a structure formed by the union of the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct. It does not involve the accessory pancreatic duct.

 

Option D. Sphincter of Oddi: Incorrect. The Sphincter of Oddi controls the flow of bile and pancreatic juices through the ampulla of Vater into the duodenum. It is unrelated to the accessory pancreatic duct.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The accessory pancreatic duct opens into the minor duodenal papilla, which is distinct from the major duodenal papilla where the main pancreatic duct terminates.

questions.stem: Which dermatome is involved in Kehr’s sign?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) C345

 

Kehr's sign refers to referred pain felt at the left shoulder tip due to irritation of the diaphragm, commonly seen in cases of splenic rupture. The diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve, which has a root value of C3, C4, and C5 (commonly remembered as "C3, C4, C5 keep the diaphragm alive").

 

When the diaphragm is irritated, such as in cases of splenic rupture, this pain is referred to the shoulder because the supraclavicular nerves, which also originate from the same root values (C3-C4), share the same sensory pathways. This phenomenon explains the referred pain observed in Kehr’s sign.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Kehr’s sign is caused by referred pain to the C3, C4, and C5 dermatomes due to irritation of the diaphragm, most commonly following splenic rupture.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the pelvic diaphragm?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B

 

The pelvic diaphragm is primarily formed by the levator ani muscle group and the coccygeus muscle, which span the pelvic cavity and act as a floor to support pelvic organs. In the provided image, the structure labeled B represents the levator ani muscle, which is the key component of the pelvic diaphragm. This diaphragm separates the pelvic cavity from the perineum and plays a crucial role in supporting the rectum, bladder, and other pelvic organs.

 

 

The levator ani muscle consists of the following parts: 

 

  1. Pubococcygeus
  2. Iliococcygeus
  3. Puborectalis

 

These muscles originate from the pubic bone, ischium, and obturator fascia, attaching posteriorly to the coccyx. Collectively, they are responsible for lifting the anus and maintaining continence.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A (Obturator internus muscle): Incorrect. This is the obturator internus, which forms the lateral wall of the pelvic cavity and is not part of the pelvic diaphragm.

 

Option C (Internal anal sphincter): Incorrect. The internal anal sphincter is a smooth muscle surrounding the anal canal and is not a component of the pelvic diaphragm.

 

Option D (External anal sphincter): Incorrect. The external anal sphincter is a voluntary muscle surrounding the anal canal but is not part of the pelvic diaphragm.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The pelvic diaphragm is formed by the levator ani muscle (pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, and puborectalis) and the coccygeus muscle, which collectively support pelvic organs and separate the pelvic cavity from the perineum.

questions.stem: A patient with positive Murphy’s sign on clinical suspicion underwent cholecystectomy. On histopathological examination the finding is normal. The gall bladder epithelium will be?
questions.solutionHtml:
Simple Columnar 

 

The gallbladder is lined by simple columnar epithelium with tall, closely packed cells specialized for absorption and secretion. This epithelium helps concentrate bile by absorbing water and electrolytes.

 

 

  • Murphy’s sign, a clinical indicator of acute cholecystitis, may lead to a suspicion of gallbladder pathology requiring cholecystectomy. However, in this case, histopathology revealed a normal gallbladder, which still retains the characteristic simple columnar epithelium without pathological changes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Squamous: Incorrect. Squamous epithelium is seen in areas like the esophagus and skin but is not present in the gallbladder.

 

Option C. Simple Columnar with brush border: Incorrect. Although both types are columnar, the gallbladder lacks the brush border (microvilli) that is characteristic of absorptive cells in the intestines.

 

Option D. Cuboidal with stereocilia: Incorrect. Cuboidal epithelium with stereocilia is typically found in the epididymis, not the gallbladder.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The normal gallbladder epithelium is simple columnar, which is essential for its function of concentrating bile through water and electrolyte absorption.

questions.stemHtml: In shown slide blank zones are due to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Fat washed in alcohol

 

The slide demonstrates adipose tissue with characteristic blank zones. These blank spaces are caused by the removal of fat (lipids) during slide preparation.

 

  • During the preparation of histology slides, the tissue is typically treated with organic solvents such as alcohol or acetone. These solvents dissolve fat because of the principle of "like dissolves like" (both are non-polar substances).
  • As the fat is washed away, it leaves empty spaces that appear as blank zones under the microscope, giving a signet ring appearance to adipocytes.

 

Stains used for fats:

 

  • Lipids can be visualized using specific fat stains like Oil Red O, Sudan Black, or Osmium Tetroxide, which are used in special preparations.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Protein washed in acetone: Incorrect. Proteins are not soluble in organic solvents like acetone and are not removed during this process.

 

Option B. Protein washed in alcohol: Incorrect. Alcohol does not dissolve proteins, so this option is not relevant to the blank zones.

 

Option C. Carbohydrate washed in acetone: Incorrect. Carbohydrates are not removed by organic solvents like acetone; this  does not fit the blank zones observed in the slide.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The blank zones in histological slides of adipose tissue are caused by fat being dissolved in alcohol or acetone during slide preparation.

questions.stemHtml: Shown artery divides in which intercostal space:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 6th

 

The artery shown in the image is the internal thoracic artery, also referred to as the internal mammary artery. This artery is a branch of the subclavian artery and travels along the inner side of the thoracic wall, adjacent to the sternum.

 

 

At the 6th intercostal space, the internal thoracic artery bifurcates into two terminal branches:

 

  1. Superior epigastric artery: This artery continues downward to supply the anterior abdominal wall.
  2. Musculophrenic artery: This artery supplies the diaphragm and gives branches to the lower intercostal spaces.

 

Additionally, the internal thoracic artery provides anterior intercostal arteries up to the 6th intercostal space, after which these branches arise from the musculophrenic artery.

 

The 6th intercostal space is a critical landmark for the division of this artery into its two branches.

 

Clinical importance:

 

  • The internal thoracic artery is the preferred artery for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) due to its excellent patency rates.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 4th: Incorrect. The internal thoracic artery does not divide at this level; it continues further downward along the thoracic wall.

 

Option B. 5th: Incorrect. The division occurs one intercostal space below this level, at the 6th intercostal space.

 

Option D. 7th: Incorrect. The bifurcation occurs at the 6th intercostal space, not the 7th.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The internal thoracic artery bifurcates into the superior epigastric artery and musculophrenic artery at the 6th intercostal space.
