Clinical importance: The internal thoracic artery is the preferred artery for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) due to its excellent patency rates. Other Options: Option A. 4th: Incorrect. The internal thoracic artery does not divide at this level; it continues further downward along the thoracic wall. Option B. 5th: Incorrect. The division occurs one intercostal space below this level, at the 6th intercostal space. Option D. 7th: Incorrect. The bifurcation occurs at the 6th intercostal space, not the 7th. Educational Objective: The internal thoracic artery bifurcates into the superior epigastric artery and musculophrenic artery at the 6th intercostal space.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statement is/ are correct for below clinical situation:

options.label: A
options.text: It is case of Meningocele, due to folic acid deficiency, which resulted in failure of closure of neural tube on 28th day of IUL.

options.label: B
options.text: It is case of Meningomyelocele, due to folic acid deficiency, which resulted in failure of closure of neural tube on 28th day of IUL.

options.label: C
options.text: It is case of Anencephaly due to folic acid deficiency, which resulted in failure of closure of neural tube on 25th day of IUL.

options.label: D
options.text: It is case of Anencephaly due to folic acid deficiency, which resulted in failure of closure of neural tube on 28th day of IUL.

questions.answerText: It is case of Anencephaly due to folic acid deficiency, which resulted in failure of closure of neural tube on 25th day of IUL.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It is case of Anencephaly due to folic acid deficiency, which resulted in failure of closure of neural tube on 25th day of IUL

 

The image depicts anencephaly, a congenital defect characterized by the absence of the cranial vault and most of the brain due to the failure of closure of the anterior neural tube. Key details include:

 

  1. Condition:
    • Anencephaly occurs when the cranial end of the neural tube fails to close.
    • This condition leads to an absent or severely underdeveloped brain and skull (cranial vault).
  2. Cause:
    • It is associated with folic acid deficiency during early pregnancy.
  3. Timing:
    • The neural tube normally closes between the 23rd and 27th day of intrauterine life (IUL). The anterior neuropore closure is completed by the 25th day of IUL.
  4. Key Features:
    • Absent cranial vault (visible in the image).
    • Exposed brain tissue, which is incompatible with life.

 

Based on the given options, C correctly identifies the condition (anencephaly), the cause (folic acid deficiency), and the timing (failure of closure on the 25th day of IUL).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is a case of Meningocele, due to folic acid deficiency, which resulted in failure of closure of the neural tube on the 28th day of IUL: This involves herniation of meninges through a defect in the vertebrae or skull. It is not the condition shown in the image.

 

Option B. It is a case of Meningomyelocele, due to folic acid deficiency, which resulted in failure of closure of the neural tube on the 28th day of IUL: This is a form of spina bifida where both meninges and spinal cord herniate, typically at the lumbosacral region, not the cranial vault.

 

Option D. It is a case of Anencephaly due to folic acid deficiency, which resulted in failure of closure of the neural tube on the 28th day of IUL: The neural tube closure for the anterior neuropore is completed by the 25th day of IUL. Hence, the timeline mentioned in this option is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Anencephaly occurs due to the failure of anterior neural tube closure by the 25th day of IUL and is strongly linked to folic acid deficiency during pregnancy.

questions.stemHtml: A 53-year-old female with recurrent medical history presented to the local emergency department with complaints of fever, headaches, and left eye swelling. The patient and her husband visited many times to their parents village at latin America, where they give history of sleeping on a bed net-covered wooden platform bed in a one-room cottage often that lacked netted windows and doors. Now she has features of dysphagia also. Barium swallow examination was done and following feature was seen as shown in image. Which of the following is responsible for this clinical situation?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of migration of neural crest cells.

options.label: B
options.text: Abnormal Hyaluronic acid activity during embryonic life

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Chronic trypanosomiasis 

 

Barium findings are suggestive of Bird’s beak sign which is seen in achalasia cardia. Which is the sign of Chagas disease. Chagas disease is caused by trypanosomiasis. Chagas disease is also known as American trypanosomiasis.


Chronic trypanosomiasis leads to serious complications involving digestive and cardiovascular systems, symptoms mentioned in the question are suggestive of involvement of these systems. Here’s a breakdown:

 

  1. Disease Background:
    • Chagas disease is transmitted by the Triatomine bug (kissing bug), commonly found in rural Latin American areas.
    • Chronic infection with Trypanosoma cruzi leads to autonomic nervous system dysfunction, specifically affecting the Auerbach's plexus, causing esophageal motility disorders like achalasia cardia.
  2. Barium Swallow Findings:
    • The "bird's beak" sign is a classic radiological feature where the distal esophagus tapers due to failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.
  3. Acute vs Chronic:
    • Acute trypanosomiasis typically presents with symptoms like fever, headaches, and a swelling near the site of the bite (e.g., Romana’s sign - periorbital swelling).
    • Chronic trypanosomiasis develops over time and causes systemic complications like achalasia, megaesophagus, or megacolon due to progressive autonomic plexus destruction.
  4. Differentiation:
    • The prolonged course and progressive development of dysphagia suggest chronic disease.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Failure of migration of neural crest cells: This is seen in congenital conditions like Hirschsprung's disease, which affects the rectum and colon, not the esophagus.

 

Option B. Abnormal Hyaluronic acid activity during embryonic life: This would be associated with congenital achalasia but does not apply to this acquired case due to infection.

 

Option C. Acute trypanosomiasis: Acute forms are more systemic and do not lead to dysphagia or achalasia. This case clearly represents chronic progression.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The bird’s beak sign on barium swallow and dysphagia in a patient from Latin America suggest achalasia cardia secondary to chronic trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease), caused by Trypanosoma cruzi infection.

questions.stem: Portal vein is formed at which vertebral level?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) L2

 

The portal vein is a crucial vessel that drains blood from the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, and spleen to the liver. It is formed by the union of the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein (SMV).

 

Formation of Portal Vein:

 

  • The splenic vein travels from the spleen, posterior to the pancreas.
    • The superior mesenteric vein approaches from in front of the uncinate process of the pancreas.
    • These two veins unite behind the neck of the pancreas, at the level of L2 vertebra, forming the portal vein.

 

Clinical Importance:

 

  • Portal vein formation occurs in close relation to the pancreas and the duodenum.
    • It is vital in conditions like portal hypertension and liver cirrhosis, where venous drainage is impaired.

 

Key Anatomical Relations:

 

  • The C-loop of the duodenum surrounds the head of the pancreas.
    • The splenic vein and SMV join behind the pancreas and are positioned near the second part of the duodenum, which corresponds to L2 vertebra.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. L1: This is the level of the first part of the duodenum, not the location of portal vein formation.

 

Option C. L3: This corresponds to the third part of the duodenum, which is lower than the portal vein's formation site.

 

Option D. L4: This is too low and is related to the abdominal aorta bifurcation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The portal vein is formed at the L2 vertebral level, behind the neck of the pancreas, by the union of the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein.

questions.stemHtml: Which structure develops from arrow marked structure shown in image:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Tonsil

 

The arrow in the image is pointing to the second pharyngeal pouch. The pharyngeal apparatus includes the arches, clefts, and pouches. The second pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the palatine tonsils.

 

Here’s how the second pouch contributes to the tonsil:

 

  • The endodermal lining of the second pharyngeal pouch proliferates to form the crypts of the palatine tonsil.
  • The surrounding mesenchyme forms the lymphoid tissue of the tonsil.

 

Other structures formed by pharyngeal pouches include:

 

  1. First pouch: Tubo-tympanic recess, which contributes to the middle ear cavity and the auditory tube.
  2. Third pouch: Dorsal part forms Parathyroid III; ventral part forms the thymus.
  3. Fourth pouch: Dorsal part forms Parathyroid IV; ventral part forms the ultimobranchial body, which contributes to the parafollicular cells of the thyroid.

 

 

 

Note:

 

Clinical Correlation:

 

  • DiGeorge Syndrome: A defect in the development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to:
    • Absence or hypoplasia of the thymus.
    • Defective development of parathyroid glands.
    • Associated with congenital heart defects.

 

Tympanic Membrane:

 

  • Unique structure that develops from all three germ layers:
    • Ectoderm: Outer layer.
    • Endoderm: Inner layer.
    • Mesoderm: Middle layer.
  • First Cleft: Forms the external auditory meatus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Tubo-tympanic recess: Incorrect. This develops from the first pharyngeal pouch, not the second.

 

Option C. Parathyroid III: Incorrect. This structure is derived from the third pharyngeal pouch, not the second.

 

Option D. Parathyroid IV: Incorrect. This structure is derived from the fourth pharyngeal pouch, not the second.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The second pharyngeal pouch forms the palatine tonsils, which are part of the lymphatic system and play a role in immune defense.

questions.stemHtml: A patient has history of splenic trauma & severe intraperitoneal bleeding. To prevent shock, you will occlude which structure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) D

 

D denotes the lienorenal ligament which contains the splenic artery. Spleen is a storehouse of blood and is supplied by a splenic artery which is the branch of the celiac trunk. In case of trauma to the spleen the splenic artery needs to be occluded in order to stop the flow of blood coming to the spleen and hence stopping the bleeding.

 

  • The splenic artery is highly tortuous and lies along the superior border of the pancreas before reaching the spleen through the splenorenal ligament.
  • Occlusion of the splenic artery cuts off the blood supply to the spleen, thereby reducing bleeding significantly.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Celiac trunk: Incorrect. While the splenic artery is a branch of the celiac trunk, occluding the celiac trunk would compromise blood supply to other organs like the liver, stomach, and pancreas, causing widespread ischemia.

 

Option C. Inferior vena cava (IVC): Incorrect. The IVC is not directly involved in the splenic blood supply. Occluding the IVC could lead to severe systemic venous congestion.

 

Option D. Aorta: Incorrect. Occluding the aorta would compromise systemic blood flow, causing life-threatening consequences.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of splenic trauma with severe bleeding, occlusion of the splenic artery within the splenorenal ligament (D) is the most effective way to prevent hemorrhagic shock.
